solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Reach one working on land and take a tumble?

parts.note: to reach a place is to come to it
a cropper is one who grows crops, a farm worker

explanation.surface: Someone arriving at a farm labourer ends up falling over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one working on land' gives A CROPPER, the article included, beside COME for 'Reach'.
explanation.definitionFit: To come a cropper is an idiom for having a heavy fall, so the phrase matches taking a tumble.

clue.text: Time in Lancashire town largely providing laugh

indicators.note: in says the time letter goes inside the shortened town name
largely means most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: Chorley is a market town in Lancashire, a county in north-west England

explanation.surface: A spell in a northern English town is said to give someone a good laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'largely' cuts CHORLEY to CHORLE, and 'in' puts T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A chortle is a gleeful chuckle, a kind of laugh, and both work as verb or noun.

clue.text: Scene with amateur in film — characterising one in unsuitable role?

indicators.note: in places scene and amateur letters inside the word for film

parts.note: a film is a thin layer, as a mist is on glass
SC is an abbreviation for scene in play scripts

explanation.surface: An amateur appearing in a film scene seems to have been given the wrong part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'film' is not a movie but a thin coating, MIST. The definition is an adjective describing an actor put in the wrong part.
explanation.definitionFit: A miscast actor has been given an unsuitable role, so the word describes such a person.

clue.text: A clique protecting others is impressive

indicators.note: protecting means one word wraps round the other, guarding it

parts.note: a ring is a close group, a clique
the rest means the others

explanation.surface: A tight group shielding outsiders makes a striking impression.
explanation.definitionFit: Arresting means striking or eye-catching, a synonym for impressive.

clue.text: Bill in residence for activity on course?

indicators.note: in puts the bill letters inside the residence abbreviation

parts.note: AC (account) is a bill

explanation.surface: A bill at home is presented to cover some activity on a course of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' suggests education but means a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Races are what happen on a racecourse, so they are the activity there, with the question mark marking the pun.

clue.text: Relate start of tale amid quiet time at home

parts.note: P is the musical notation piano, meaning quiet

indicators.note: amid says the first letter goes among the other pieces

parts.note: an era is a period of time

indicators.note: start of picks out the first letter of tale

parts.note: in means at home

explanation.surface: Begin telling a story during a peaceful spell spent at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relate' is the verb here, as in 'this relates to that', not telling a story.
explanation.definitionFit: To pertain to something is to relate or belong to it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: English test I've found contrary to reason?

parts.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for vehicles in Britain
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A test of English that someone sat seems to defy logic.
explanation.walkthrough: MOT is the annual safety test British cars must pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotive means appealing to feeling rather than logic, so it runs counter to reason, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Son traced kit worn as staple resource

indicators.note: worn suggests the letters have been battered out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy's kit, traced and worn, is described as his basic equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worn' is the anagram signal on SON TRACED KIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock-in-trade is an idiom for the basic goods or skills one relies on, a staple resource.

clue.text: Appropriate reduction in garment?

indicators.note: reduction in says the word for the garment is cut short by one letter

parts.note: trousers are a garment

explanation.surface: A suitable shortening for a piece of clothing is proposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like an adjective (suitable) but is the verb meaning to pocket; dropping the last S from TROUSERS gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser money is slang for pocketing it, often dishonestly, which is to appropriate it.

clue.text: Odd copper in front of us touring port

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the pair surrounds the port
in front of puts the copper symbol before the word us

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
taken as written
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port, Rio for short

explanation.surface: A strange copper travels round a port ahead of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' wraps the copper symbol and 'us', taken together, round the port; 'in front of' fixes their order.
explanation.definitionFit: Curious can mean strange or peculiar, the same sense as odd.

clue.text: Second girl on edge about a daring sportsman?

indicators.note: on means placed before, in a down clue on top of

parts.note: Kate is a girl's name

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the edge word goes round the letter

parts.note: a border is an edge

explanation.surface: Briefly, a girl teetering on a brink is imagined as some bold athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts A inside BORDER to give BOARDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A skateboarder performs risky tricks on a board, so is a daring sporting type; the question mark admits this is loose.

clue.text: Sword hurt girl

parts.note: to cut someone is to hurt them
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A blade has wounded a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutlass is a short curved sword once used by sailors.

clue.text: It's a man revitalised showing endurance

indicators.note: revitalised means given new life, so the letters are remade in a new order

explanation.surface: A man given fresh energy shows he can keep going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revitalised' signals the anagram of IT'S A MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is staying power, the capacity to endure.

clue.text: Foolish writer on reflection restricted by drink

indicators.note: restricted by means held within the drink word

parts.note: It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

indicators.note: on reflection means seen as in a mirror, so the writer word runs backwards

parts.note: a pen is a writer

explanation.surface: A writer thinking back is held back by alcohol and behaves foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drink' is the vermouth in a gin and It, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept means clumsy or lacking judgment, which can be called foolish.

clue.text: Cite sinner sadly with no end of cant as hypocritical

indicators.note: sadly suggests the words are in a sorry state and must be rearranged
end of picks the last letter of cant, which is taken away from the pool

explanation.surface: Quoting a wrongdoer with regret while avoiding pious talk sounds two-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes T, the last letter of 'cant', from CITE SINNER; 'sadly' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Insincere means not genuine in feeling, a close synonym of hypocritical.

clue.text: Spare chap working in rubbish site

indicators.note: working means being worked on, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A spare man is employed at the local tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' signals the anagram of SPARE CHAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrapheap is a pile of discarded junk, a place where rubbish is dumped.

clue.text: Gunners unfurled flag held by sailor in battle

indicators.note: held by means placed inside the sailor word

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners of the British Army

indicators.note: unfurled means spread out, so the letters of flag are rearranged

explanation.surface: Artillerymen unroll a flag that a seaman holds during a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfurled' scrambles 'flag'; the Gunners here are the Royal Artillery, not the football club Arsenal.
explanation.definitionFit: Trafalgar was the 1805 naval battle in which Nelson defeated the French and Spanish fleets.

clue.text: Amount of land about to be acquired by a prison

indicators.note: to be acquired by means taken into the prison word

parts.note: a cage is a prison
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A plot of ground is about to be taken over by a jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like a container signal but is the short word meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Acreage is land measured in acres, an amount of land.

clue.text: A look about policeman beginning to prohibit drink for youngsters

indicators.note: about means going round, so the look word surrounds the policeman

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look
a cop is a policeman

indicators.note: beginning to picks out the first letter of prohibit

explanation.surface: A policeman keeps watch over the start of a ban on sweet drinks for teens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look' gives the archaic exclamation, as in 'lo and behold'.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcopop is a sweet, fizzy alcoholic drink marketed at young drinkers.

clue.text: Dog given lead in park by much of Bedfordshire town

indicators.note: lead in picks out the first letter of park
much of means most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: Luton is a large town in Bedfordshire, a county north of London

explanation.surface: A dog is walked on its lead in a park by a town in Bedfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' looks like a dog's leash but means the first letter. 'much of' cuts LUTON to LUTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluto is the name of Mickey Mouse's pet dog in Disney cartoons.

clue.text: Pepper, worthless stuff put on a drink served up

indicators.note: put on means placed above, in a down clue on top of what follows

parts.note: pap is trivial or worthless material

indicators.note: served up means brought upwards, so in a down entry the drink word reads backwards

parts.note: kir is a drink of white wine and cassis

explanation.surface: Some rubbish is placed on a drink that comes to the table.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'served up' reads the drink from bottom to top; kir is white wine with blackcurrant liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: Paprika is a powdered red pepper used as a spice.

clue.text: Lone soul surprisingly left out and set free

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests the letters end up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A solitary person, unexpectedly abandoned, is released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes L (left) from LONE SOUL; 'surprisingly' rearranges the remaining seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To unloose is to release or let go, so it means to set free.

clue.text: A vessel holding a lot of cereal and fruit

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the vessel goes round the cereal

parts.note: a pot is a vessel

indicators.note: a lot of means most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: rice is a cereal

explanation.surface: A pot holds a good deal of grain as well as some fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit.

clue.text: Some vote ethically showing effective force

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Voting with principles shows real power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' signals the letters hidden across 'voTE ETHically'.
explanation.definitionFit: Teeth is used figuratively for real power to enforce, as in a law with teeth.

clue.text: London suburb containing university that's well liked

indicators.note: containing means the suburb name holds the university letter

parts.note: Poplar is a district of east London

explanation.surface: A London district with a university proves a favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: POPLAR is a district in east London.
explanation.definitionFit: Popular means widely liked or admired, the same as well liked.

clue.text: Second book in short sufficient as specimen

parts.note: Exodus, the second book of the Bible, is abbreviated Ex
ample means enough or sufficient

explanation.surface: A second volume, briefly, is plenty as a sample.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second book' is Exodus, the Bible's second book, and 'in short' abbreviates it to EX.
explanation.definitionFit: An example is one item representing a type, which is what a specimen is.

clue.text: Part of serial is appearing after record and poem

indicators.note: appearing after places the word is behind the record letters

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
an ode is a poem

explanation.surface: A section of a serialised work comes after a recording and some verse.
explanation.definitionFit: An episode is one instalment of a serial on radio or television.

clue.text: Retrospective look by the man on board, we hear, to prevent contention

indicators.note: retrospective means looking backwards, so the look word is read in reverse

parts.note: a peek is a quick look
taken as written

indicators.note: we hear says the chess word is spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: a chessman on the board is a piece

explanation.surface: A man looks back on a board meeting to stop an argument breaking out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' reverses PEEK to KEEP; 'by' joins it to THE, and 'we hear' turns PIECE into its sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep the peace is an idiom for avoiding or stopping quarrels, so preventing contention.
